name: Wild Bergamot / Bee Balm
habitat: Dry to moderately moist open ground across most of North America — tallgrass prairie, glade and rocky woodland margins, unplanted fields, fencerows and roadsides in full sun.
parts: Leaves and the shaggy lavender-pink flower heads, fresh or dried. Carvacrol and thymol give it an oregano-and-thyme flavor: good in bean and tomato dishes, meat rubs, and steeped as tea. Roots are not used. Confirm three things before picking — a square, hollow stem, opposite toothed grayish-green leaves, and a strong oregano smell from a crushed leaf.

lookalikes.name: Spotted horsemint (Monarda punctata)
lookalikes.tell: Same genus, same square stem and aromatic leaf, but its flowers are pale yellow blotched with purple, stacked in whorls above showy pink-and-white bracts down the stem. Its thymol content is high enough to taste harsh and medicinal rather than pleasant. Wild bergamot carries a single shaggy lavender-pink pompom at the top of the stem.

harvest: Cut the top third of flowering stems with scissors and leave the rest standing. Wild bergamot is a first-rank nectar plant for bees, hummingbirds and butterflies, and native bees nest inside the hollow dead stems over winter — so leave dead stems up. Take from large stands only, never more than a small fraction, and leave plenty of flowers to set seed.
